page_contents_html:
Dyspepsia is a clinical syndrome characterised by epigastric pain or discomfort, bloating, early satiety, nausea, or heartburn. It affects an estimated 25–40% of adults and accounts for a significant proportion of GP consultations.

Key subtypes:

  • Uninvestigated dyspepsia — symptoms without prior endoscopy
  • GORD — heartburn/regurgitation predominant, often without structural pathology
  • H. pylori-associated dyspepsia — caused by or complicated by Helicobacter pylori infection
  • Functional (non-ulcer) dyspepsia — persistent symptoms with negative investigations
  • Peptic ulcer disease — gastric or duodenal ulcer, often H. pylori-related or NSAID-related

What must not be missed:

  • Upper GI malignancy (gastric, oesophageal)
  • Peptic ulcer with bleeding or perforation
  • Cardiac disease mimicking dyspepsia

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
History

  • Duration, onset, character, and location of symptoms
  • Relationship to food, posture, alcohol, smoking, and caffeine
  • Current medications: NSAIDs, aspirin, bisphosphonates, iron, SSRIs, calcium channel blockers
  • Previous H. pylori testing or eradication; previous endoscopy findings
  • Family history of upper GI cancer
  • Unintentional weight loss, dysphagia, odynophagia — if present, see Who to refer

Examination

  • Document weight (assess for unintentional loss)
  • Abdominal palpation: epigastric tenderness, palpable mass
  • Signs of anaemia: pallor, koilonychia
  • Left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Virchow's node — raises suspicion of gastric malignancy)

Red flags — action required urgently (see Who to refer)

  • Haematemesis or melaena
  • Dysphagia or odynophagia (any age)
  • Persistent vomiting
  • Unintentional weight loss
  • Epigastric mass on examination
  • Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia
  • Age ≥55 with new, unexplained, or treatment-refractory dyspepsia

H. pylori testing

  • Preferred test: faecal antigen test — do not use serology (not validated for active infection) and avoid office-based serological tests
  • Urea breath test is an acceptable alternative where locally available
  • Washout period: stop PPI for at least 2 weeks before testing; stop antibiotics for at least 4 weeks before testing
  • Test before starting empirical PPI in uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features
  • Confirm eradication: retest by faecal antigen test or urea breath test at least 6–8 weeks after completing eradication therapy (do not use serology to confirm eradication)

NSAID review

  • Review indication for any NSAID or aspirin and consider stopping or substituting with paracetamol-based analgesia
  • If NSAID must continue: switch to lowest-dose COX-2 selective agent and add a PPI; review every 6 months
  • Always test for H. pylori in NSAID users with dyspepsia and eradicate if positive

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
Uninvestigated dyspepsia (no alarm features, age <55)

  1. Test for H. pylori using faecal antigen test (after PPI washout)
  2. If H. pylori positive: offer 7-day triple eradication therapy (see below)
  3. If H. pylori negative, or symptoms persist after successful eradication: offer empirical full-dose PPI for 4 weeks
  4. Review response at 4–8 weeks; step down to lowest effective dose or as-needed use
  5. If symptoms recur: re-introduce PPI at lowest effective dose; annual review for long-term users

GORD (heartburn/regurgitation predominant)

  • Full-dose PPI for 4–8 weeks
  • Severe oesophagitis: full-dose PPI for 8 weeks; maintain at full dose long-term
  • Step down to lowest effective dose once controlled; consider as-needed use for mild symptoms

H. pylori eradication — first-line (7 days, all doses twice-daily)

  • Standard: PPI + Amoxicillin 1g + Clarithromycin 500mg
  • Alternative (if metronidazole preferred or clarithromycin resistance likely): PPI + Amoxicillin 1g + Metronidazole 400mg
  • Penicillin-allergic: PPI + Clarithromycin 500mg + Metronidazole 400mg
  • Prior clarithromycin exposure: PPI + Bismuth subsalicylate + Metronidazole + Tetracycline

H. pylori eradication — second-line (7 days, if first-line fails)

  • PPI + Amoxicillin + whichever of Clarithromycin or Metronidazole was NOT used first-line
  • Exposed to both clarithromycin and metronidazole: PPI + Amoxicillin + Tetracycline (or levofloxacin — check fluoroquinolone restrictions)
  • Penicillin-allergic, no fluoroquinolone exposure: PPI + Metronidazole + levofloxacin (note: SMC/SIGN fluoroquinolone restrictions apply)
  • Penicillin-allergic with fluoroquinolone exposure: PPI + Bismuth subsalicylate + Metronidazole + Tetracycline
  • After second-line failure: refer to gastroenterology — do not prescribe third-line empirically

PPI choice for eradication regimens: Omeprazole 20mg twice-daily or Lansoprazole 30mg twice-daily are standard — confirm current D&G formulary first choice.

NSAID-associated dyspepsia

  • Stop NSAID where clinically possible
  • If continuation required: switch to COX-2 selective agent at lowest effective dose and add a PPI
  • Test for H. pylori and eradicate if positive
  • Review NSAID indication at every contact; aim to step down or stop

Lifestyle advice (all dyspepsia)

  • Smoking cessation
  • Alcohol moderation
  • Weight loss if overweight
  • Avoid trigger foods (fatty food, spice, citrus, caffeine)
  • Eat smaller, more frequent meals; avoid eating within 3 hours of bedtime
  • Elevate head of bed by 15–20cm (for GORD/nocturnal symptoms)

Follow-up

  • Review response at 4–8 weeks
  • Gastric ulcer confirmed on OGD: arrange repeat endoscopy 6–8 weeks after starting treatment to confirm healing and exclude malignancy
  • Peptic ulcer with H. pylori: retest for eradication using faecal antigen test or breath test at 6–8 weeks post-treatment
  • Long-term PPI users: annual review; encourage step-down or as-needed use

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Same-day referral / emergency

  • Haematemesis (vomiting blood)
  • Melaena (black tarry stool)
  • Signs of upper GI perforation (acute abdomen, peritonism)

Admit same-day via A&E or call 999 if haemodynamically unstable. Suspend NSAIDs immediately.

Urgent 2-week-wait OGD (suspected upper GI cancer — NICE NG12)

  • Age ≥55 with unexplained weight loss AND any of: upper abdominal pain, reflux, or dyspepsia
  • Age ≥55 with treatment-refractory dyspepsia
  • Age ≥55 with upper abdominal mass
  • Dysphagia — any age, refer urgently
  • Haematemesis — any age (if not requiring same-day emergency admission)

Refer via SCI referral / Choose Well urgent pathway. Suspend NSAIDs at point of referral. Consider whether patient is fit for endoscopy before referring.

Routine gastroenterology referral

  • Symptoms unresponsive to adequate trial of H. pylori eradication AND full-dose PPI
  • H. pylori not eradicated after second-line therapy (for culture, sensitivity testing, and third-line treatment)
  • Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia not explained by another cause (routine or urgent depending on clinical context)
  • Patient requesting consideration of anti-reflux surgery (laparoscopic fundoplication) for GORD
  • Barrett's oesophagus requiring surveillance coordination
  • Diagnostic uncertainty where endoscopy is needed but criteria for urgent referral are not met

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
The following presentations should be managed in primary care and do not require routine gastroenterology referral:

  • Uncomplicated dyspepsia in patients aged <55 with no alarm features — test for H. pylori, eradicate if positive, trial PPI; manage fully in primary care
  • H. pylori-positive dyspepsia — treat with first-line eradication; confirm eradication; refer only if eradication fails after two courses
  • GORD well-controlled on PPI — continue in primary care with annual review and stepdown attempts; no referral needed unless refractory or surgical review requested
  • Functional (non-ulcer) dyspepsia — once upper GI malignancy excluded by age and alarm feature assessment, manage in primary care (PPI, lifestyle, consider low-dose tricyclic antidepressant if refractory)
  • Dyspepsia in pregnancy — manage with lifestyle advice and antacids; refer only if severe, atypical, or unresponsive
  • NSAID-induced dyspepsia where stopping the NSAID resolves symptoms — no further investigation required
  • Confirmed peptic ulcer responding to H. pylori eradication — manage in primary care; arrange post-treatment endoscopy for gastric ulcers locally rather than referring to gastroenterology
  • Incidental hiatus hernia on imaging without significant GORD symptoms — does not require referral
